paragraphs.text: Pseudohypoaldosteronism type I is a salt-wasting disorder caused by target organ unresponsiveness to mineralocorticoids. It presents in the newborn with renal salt wasting, dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis, even though aldosterone levels are high. The autosomal dominant or sporadic form is milder than the autosomal recessive form, involves only the kidney, and remits with age (Hanukoglu, 1991; Geller et al., 1998).

checks.evidence_quote: Type I pseudohypoaldosteronism (PHA) is a hereditary disease characterized by salt wasting resulting from target organ unresponsiveness to mineralocorticoids.

paragraphs.text: Armanini et al. (1985) studied 3 patients with pseudohypoaldosteronism: a 28-year-old index case in Melbourne and 2 sibs in Munich, aged 8 and 2 years, whose parents were first cousins. The younger sib, a boy, was less severely affected clinically than his sister. The authors described the syndrome as salt wasting and failure to thrive, usually presenting in infancy with high urinary sodium despite hyponatremia, together with hyperkalemia, hyperreninemia, and elevated aldosterone levels.

paragraphs.text: Hanukoglu (1991) studied 2 kindreds with a total of 9 patients with PHA. In kindred I, the proband presented in infancy with renal salt wasting: vomiting, failure to thrive, short stature, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia. The proband responded dramatically to a high-salt diet (2.5 g/day), and sodium supplementation was stopped at age 2 years. In 7 more members of the family across 3 generations, clinical expression of PHA ranged from none to moderate. In the affected members (the proband, the mother, and 2 brothers), hyperaldosteronism persisted for 13 years, whereas plasma renin activity gradually fell to near-normal values. Hanukoglu (1991) took this pattern to indicate tertiary hyperaldosteronism caused by an autonomously functioning zona glomerulosa. In kindred II, the proband was born to consanguineous parents and developed severe renal salt loss at age 9 days. She also had raised salivary and sweat electrolytes, consistent with unresponsiveness to mineralocorticoids in multiple organs. Life-threatening salt-wasting episodes recurred after age 2 years, and at age 5 years she still needed 14 g/day of salt supplements. A sister had died at 9 days of age with symptoms of PHA.

They described the disorder as neonatal salt loss with dehydration, hypotension, hyperkalemia, and metabolic acidosis despite elevated plasma aldosterone levels and plasma renin activity. In the autosomal dominant form, salt wasting is milder and gradually improves with age.

paragraphs.text: Armanini et al. (1985) looked for abnormal type I ('mineralocorticoid-like') receptors in mononuclear leukocytes from 3 patients with pseudohypoaldosteronism. In control monocytes, [3H]aldosterone was bound with high affinity (Kd approximately 3 nM) at 150 to 600 sites per cell. On repeated testing, monocytes from 2 of the patients showed no [3H]aldosterone binding. The third patient, who was less severely affected, had 62 sites per cell, more than 2 SD below the control value. Binding was normal in the parents of the 2 sibs. The authors concluded that pseudohypoaldosteronism is caused by a defect in the type I receptor, which may be complete or partial.

paragraphs.text: Sartorato et al. (2003) found NR3C2 mutations in 70% of their familial cases of autosomal dominant PHA1. They considered that the absence of mutations in some families calls for extensive study of the NR3C2 gene and precise diagnostic procedures, so that other genes possibly involved in the disease can be identified.

paragraphs.text: In all affected members of a Japanese family with renal PHA1, Tajima et al. Aldosterone did not increase reporter activity in transfected COS-1 cells expressing the mutant receptor. The authors stated that this was the first missense mutation in the NR3C2 gene reported in renal PHA1.

paragraphs.text: Sartorato et al. (2003) analyzed the NR3C2 gene in 14 families with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1 and detected 6 heterozygous mutations. Two frameshift mutations in exon 2 (insT1354 and del8bp537) and a nonsense mutation in exon 4 (C645X) produce truncated proteins. Three missense mutations (G633R, Q776R, and L979P) affected receptor function in different ways. L979P had a transdominant negative effect on wildtype receptor activity, whereas G633R and Q776R probably cause PHA1 through haploinsufficiency.

paragraphs.text: In 6 patients with PHA1, Riepe et al. (2006) detected 6 heterozygous NR3C2 mutations. One frameshift mutation (c.1131dupT) had been reported before. A second frameshift mutation was c.2871dupC. There were 2 novel nonsense mutations that produce a truncated receptor protein, and 2 missense mutations, S818L and E972G. The authors studied aldosterone binding, transactivation, nuclear translocation, proteolysis, and 3-dimensional modeling to assess the functional effects of the mutations.

paragraphs.text: Cheek and Perry (1958) first described PHA type I as a salt-wasting syndrome in infancy caused by a defective renal tubular response to mineralocorticoids. Donnell et al. (1959) reported renal sodium loss, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia that they attributed to renal tubular insensitivity to mineralocorticoids, and they called the condition 'pseudohypo-adrenalocorticism.' Raine and Roy (1962) also described a salt-losing syndrome in infancy, which they called pseudohypoadrenocorticalism. Hanukoglu et al. (1978) wrote about the inheritance of pseudohypoaldosteronism.

checks.claim: Cheek and Perry (1958) first described PHA type I as a salt-wasting syndrome in infancy caused by a defective renal tubular response to mineralocorticoids.
checks.evidence_quote: A salt wasting syndrome in infancy.
checks.explanation: Only the title was supplied. It supports a salt-wasting syndrome in infancy. The claims that this was the first description of PHA type I and that the cause was a defective renal tubular response to mineralocorticoids come only from a later paper's summary (Al Thiabat et al., 2025), not from this paper's own text.

checks.evidence_quote: renal sodium loss, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia due to a renal tubular insensitivity to mineralocorticoids

checks.claim: Donnell et al. (1959) called the condition 'pseudohypo-adrenalocorticism.'
checks.evidence_quote: Pseudohypo-adrenalocorticism; renal sodium loss, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia
checks.explanation: The title uses the term 'pseudohypo-adrenalocorticism' for the condition.

checks.claim: Raine and Roy (1962) described a salt-losing syndrome in infancy that they called pseudohypoadrenocorticalism.
checks.evidence_quote: A salt-losing syndrome in infancy. Pseudo-hypoadrenocorticalism.
checks.explanation: The title says Raine and Roy described a salt-losing syndrome in infancy and named it pseudo-hypoadrenocorticalism.

checks.evidence_quote: Inheritance of pseudohypoaldosteronism.
checks.explanation: Only the title was supplied, and it directly shows that the paper is about the inheritance of pseudohypoaldosteronism.

paragraphs.text: In all affected members of a Japanese family with renal PHA1, Tajima et al. (2000) identified a heterozygous mutation that changes codon 924 from CTG (leu) to CCG (pro), a leu924-to-pro (L924P) substitution. In COS-1 cells cotransfected with a glucocorticoid response element-tk-CAT reporter, aldosterone increased CAT activity when the wildtype receptor was expressed but had no effect when the mutant receptor was expressed.

paragraphs.text: In a sporadic case of PHA1, Viemann et al. (2001) identified a heterozygous frameshift mutation in exon 9 of the NR3C2 gene, a 1-bp insertion (Ins2871C). The mutation affects the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain. Asymptomatic family members did not carry it.

checks.explanation: The frameshift, exon 9 and Ins2871C (an insertion of one C, so a 1-bp insertion) are supported. The abstract does not say the mutation was heterozygous, and only the abstract was supplied.

checks.claim: The NR3C2 Ins2871C mutation affects the last 27 amino acids of the hormone-binding domain.

paragraphs.text: In a family with autosomal dominant or sporadic PHA1, Sartorato et al. (2003) identified a heterozygous gly633-to-arg (G633R) mutation in the DNA-binding domain of the NR3C2 gene. Maximal transactivation by the mutant receptor was reduced, but its binding characteristics and the ED50 of transactivation were similar to those of the wildtype receptor. The authors suggested that the mutation probably causes PHA1 through haploinsufficiency.

paragraphs.text: In a patient with PHA1, Riepe et al. (2006) identified a heterozygous ser818-to-leu (S818L) mutation in the NR3C2 gene. The mutant receptor did not bind aldosterone, did not activate transcription, and did not translocate into the nucleus. Three-dimensional modeling showed a major displacement of several residues involved in aldosterone binding.
